- **Pivoting rows into columns:** the engagements table stores one row per interaction with a `type`. **Conditional aggregation** — `SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'X' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` — turns those row-values into separate columns, counting each type in a single pass.
- **Why `LEFT JOIN` matters:** a post with zero engagements (none here, but the pattern must handle it) would vanish under an `INNER JOIN`. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every post; its `CASE` expressions all evaluate to `0`, so it correctly reports `0` likes/comments/shares instead of disappearing.
- `GROUP BY p.post_id` collapses each post's engagement rows into one summary row.
- 💡 On MySQL you can shorten each measure to `SUM(e.engagement_type = 'LIKE')` — a boolean condition evaluates to `1`/`0` — but the explicit `CASE` form is clearer and portable across databases.

interview-questions-interview-set-3-q1.title: Find the Nth highest salary
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q1.description: Find the **2nd highest** salary from the `employees` table (the solution must generalize to any *N*).
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q1.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE Employee (
    emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    emp_name VARCHAR(50),
    salary INT
);

INSERT INTO Employee VALUES
(1,'Ravi Kumar',90000),
(2,'Anita Sharma',85000),
(3,'Vikram Singh',85000),
(4,'Neha Joshi',70000),
(5,'Suresh Rao',60000);
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q1.explanation:
- **Why wrap it in an outer `SELECT (...)`?** This is the key trick for **NULL handling**. A bare `... LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` returns an *empty result set* when there is no Nth salary (e.g. asking for the 10th highest in a 5-row table). Wrapping it as a **scalar subquery** guarantees exactly one row back — the value if it exists, otherwise a clean `NULL`. Interviewers love this because "return NULL, not zero rows" is the correct, defensive behaviour.
- **`LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1`:** after sorting salaries high→low (`90000, 85000, 85000, 70000, 60000`), we skip the first row (`OFFSET 1`) and take one (`LIMIT 1`) → `85000`. For the *Nth* highest, use `OFFSET N-1`. (Add `DISTINCT` inside if the top salary itself could be tied and you want the 2nd *distinct* value.)
- **`ROW_NUMBER()` version** makes *N* an explicit parameter (`WHERE ranking = N`) and is easy to reason about: it numbers salaries `1, 2, 3, …` descending, so `ranking = 2` is the runner-up. Here `90000` is unique, so row 2 is `85000` — matching the expected output. Swap to `DENSE_RANK()` if you specifically want the *Nth distinct* salary and the higher salaries may contain ties.
- Edge case worth stating out loud: if *N* exceeds the number of rows, both scalar-subquery forms return **`NULL`** rather than erroring or returning nothing.

interview-questions-interview-set-3-q2.title: Find duplicate records based on email
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q2.description: Find all email addresses that appear more than once in the `users` table.
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q2.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE users (
    user_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_name VARCHAR(50),
    email VARCHAR(100)
);

INSERT INTO users VALUES
(1,'Ravi Kumar','ravi@example.com'),
(2,'Anita Sharma','anita@example.com'),
(3,'Ravi K','ravi@example.com'),
(4,'Neha Joshi','neha@example.com'),
(5,'Anita S','anita@example.com');
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q2.solutionSql:
SELECT
    email,
    COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q2.explanation:
- **`GROUP BY email`** collapses all rows sharing an email into one group; **`COUNT(*)`** tells you how big each group is.
- **`HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`** keeps only groups with duplicates. Recall the ordering: `WHERE` filters *rows before* grouping, `HAVING` filters *groups after* aggregation — since `COUNT(*)` is an aggregate, it can only live in `HAVING`.
- `ravi@example.com` (rows 1 & 3) and `anita@example.com` (rows 2 & 5) each appear twice; `neha@example.com` appears once and is dropped.
- 💡 If you need the actual duplicate *rows* (not just the emails), wrap this as a subquery: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email IN (SELECT email FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)`.

interview-questions-interview-set-3-q3.solutionSql:
WITH duplicate_ranking AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        email,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY user_id) AS ranking
    FROM users
)
DELETE FROM users
WHERE user_id IN (
    SELECT user_id
    FROM duplicate_ranking
    WHERE ranking > 1
);
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q3.explanation:
- **CTE approach (preferred):** `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY user_id)` numbers rows `1, 2, …` within each email, smallest id first. Row `1` is the keeper; anything with `ranking > 1` is a duplicate. The CTE lists those ids and the `DELETE` removes them (rows 3 and 5). This reads top-to-bottom and makes the keep-one rule explicit.
- ⚠️ **MySQL quirk that this sidesteps:** you can't `DELETE FROM users WHERE user_id IN (SELECT ... FROM users)` that references the *same* table directly. Naming the subquery as a **CTE** (`duplicate_ranking`) — like a derived table — gets MySQL to materialize it first, so the delete is allowed. That's why the ranking lives in a `WITH` block rather than inline.
- **Self-join approach:** joining `users` to itself on the same email while requiring `u1.user_id > u2.user_id` matches every row that has *a smaller-id twin with the same email*. Those larger-id rows (3 and 5) are exactly the duplicates; the smallest-id copy of each email has no smaller twin, so it survives. `DELETE u1` targets only the left alias.
- **Keep-one direction:** both keep the *smallest* id. Flip to `ranking` on `ORDER BY user_id DESC` (or `u1.user_id < u2.user_id` in the self-join) to keep the *largest* / most recent instead.

interview-questions-interview-set-3-q4.title: Employees earning more than their manager
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q4.description: Find employees whose salary is higher than their direct manager's salary.
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q4.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE companyEmployee (
    emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    emp_name VARCHAR(50),
    salary INT,
    manager_id INT   -- references companyEmployee.emp_id; NULL for the CEO
);

INSERT INTO companyEmployee VALUES
(1,'Ravi Kumar',60000,NULL),
(2,'Anita Sharma',80000,1),
(3,'Vikram Singh',50000,1),
(4,'Neha Joshi',70000,2),
(5,'Suresh Rao',90000,2);
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q4.solutionSql:
SELECT
    e.emp_name  AS employee,
    e.salary    AS employee_salary,
    m.emp_name  AS manager,
    m.salary    AS manager_salary
FROM companyEmployee e
JOIN companyEmployee m
    ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q4.explanation:
- This is a **self-join on a hierarchical (self-referencing) table**. Alias `e` is the *employee*, alias `m` is the *manager*; joining `e.manager_id = m.emp_id` pairs each employee with their boss's row.
- **`WHERE e.salary > m.salary`** keeps only pairs where the subordinate out-earns the manager.
- Walking the data: Anita (80k) reports to Ravi (60k) ✅; Suresh (90k) reports to Anita (80k) ✅; Vikram (50k < 60k) and Neha (70k < 80k) don't qualify. Ravi (the CEO) has `manager_id = NULL`, so the `JOIN` drops him entirely — correct, since he has no manager to compare against.
- 💡 Note the `INNER JOIN` naturally excludes the top-level manager. If you wanted to *list* the CEO too, you'd switch to a `LEFT JOIN` — but for "earns more than manager," excluding them is exactly right.

interview-questions-interview-set-3-q5.title: Employees earning more than the department average
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q5.description: Find employees whose salary is above the average salary **of their own department**.
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q5.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE dept_staff (
    emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    emp_name VARCHAR(50),
    department VARCHAR(30),
    salary INT
);

INSERT INTO dept_staff VALUES
(1,'Ravi Kumar','Sales',50000),
(2,'Anita Sharma','Sales',70000),
(3,'Vikram Singh','IT',90000),
(4,'Neha Joshi','IT',60000),
(5,'Suresh Rao','IT',60000);
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q5.solutionSql:
SELECT
    e.emp_name,
    e.department,
    e.salary,
    (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM dept_staff d WHERE d.department = e.department) AS dept_avg
FROM dept_staff e
WHERE e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary)
    FROM dept_staff d
    WHERE d.department = e.department
);
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q5.explanation:
- **Correlated subquery:** for each outer row, the inner query recomputes `AVG(salary)` *filtered to that row's department* (`d.department = e.department`). It's "correlated" because the inner query depends on the outer row — it re-runs per row.
- **Window-function version** is cleaner and usually faster: `AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)` computes each department's average once and attaches it to every row *without collapsing rows* (unlike `GROUP BY`). We can't put a window function in `WHERE` directly, so we compute it in a subquery `t` and filter in the outer query.
- The math: Sales avg = (50k + 70k)/2 = **60k** → only Anita (70k) is above. IT avg = (90k + 60k + 60k)/3 = **70k** → only Vikram (90k) is above. Ravi, Neha, and Suresh sit at or below their department average and are excluded.
- `AVG()` returns a decimal in MySQL, hence `60000.0000`.

interview-questions-interview-set-3-q6.title: Month-over-Month sales growth
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q6.description: For each month, compute total sales and the **month-over-month growth percentage** versus the previous month.
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q6.solutionSql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT
        DATE_FORMAT(sale_date, '%Y-%m') AS sales_month,
        SUM(amount) AS total_sales
    FROM monthly_sales
    GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(sale_date, '%Y-%m')
)
SELECT
    sales_month,
    total_sales,
    LAG(total_sales) OVER (ORDER BY sales_month) AS prev_month_sales,
    ROUND(
        (total_sales - LAG(total_sales) OVER (ORDER BY sales_month))
        / LAG(total_sales) OVER (ORDER BY sales_month) * 100
    , 2) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY sales_month;
interview-questions-interview-set-3-q6.explanation:
- **Step 1 — bucket by month:** the `monthly` CTE aggregates daily rows into monthly totals using `DATE_FORMAT(sale_date, '%Y-%m')` (January's two rows, 6000 + 4000, roll up to **10000**).
- **Step 2 — reach back one month:** `LAG(total_sales) OVER (ORDER BY sales_month)` pulls the *previous* month's total onto the current row. The first month has no predecessor, so `LAG` returns `NULL` — which correctly propagates to a `NULL` growth for January.
- **Step 3 — growth formula:** `(current − previous) / previous × 100`, rounded to 2 decimals. Feb = (15000 − 10000)/10000 × 100 = **+50.00%**; Mar = (12000 − 15000)/15000 × 100 = **−20.00%**; Apr rebounds to **+50.00%**; May halves to **−50.00%**; June is flat versus May, so growth is exactly **0.00%** (a useful reminder that `0` is a real value, distinct from January's `NULL` "no prior month").
- ⚠️ **Gotchas to mention:** (1) dividing by the previous month risks a **division-by-zero** if a month had `0` sales — guard with `NULLIF(prev, 0)` in production. (2) This only works when every month is present; **missing months** silently compare non-adjacent periods. For gap-safe growth, join against a generated calendar of months.

interview-questions-interview-set-4-q1.title: Revenue per customer across four tables
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q1.description: Compute the **total revenue** (Σ quantity × unit price) for every customer, joining `customers → orders → order_items → products`. Customers with no orders must still appear, with revenue `0`.
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q1.solutionSql:
SELECT c.name,
  COALESCE(SUM(oi.qty * p.price), 0) AS total_revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o       ON c.id          = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id    = oi.order_id
LEFT JOIN products p     ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q1.explanation:
- **Chain the joins in dependency order:** each table hangs off a key in the one before it (`customer → order → item → product`). The line item's money lives across two tables — `order_items.qty` and `products.price` — so revenue is `SUM(oi.qty * p.price)`.
- **Why every join is `LEFT`:** the moment one link is `INNER`, a customer with no orders (Carol) vanishes from the result. `LEFT JOIN` all the way down keeps her; her item/price columns are `NULL`, `SUM` of nothing is `NULL`, and **`COALESCE(..., 0)`** turns that into a clean `0`.
- **Group by the customer, not the join grain:** the join explodes to one row per line item; `GROUP BY c.id` collapses it back. Alice = order 101 (2×100 + 1×50 = 250) + order 102 (1×100 = 100) = **350**; Bob = order 103 (3×200 = **600**).
- 💡 Group by `c.id` (the key), including `c.name` for display — safe even under `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` because `name` is functionally dependent on the primary key `id`.

interview-questions-interview-set-4-q2.title: Median salary of all employees
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q2.description: Find the **median** salary across all employees. Handle both odd and even total counts (even → average of the two middle values). MySQL has no built-in `MEDIAN()`.
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q2.solutionSql:
SELECT AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM (
  SELECT salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS ranking,
    COUNT(*)     OVER ()                AS total
  FROM emp2
) t
WHERE ranking IN (FLOOR((total + 1) / 2),
                  FLOOR((total + 2) / 2));
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q2.explanation:
- **Rank + size in one pass:** `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary)` numbers salaries `1..n` from lowest to highest; `COUNT(*) OVER ()` (empty `OVER()` = whole table) tags every row with the total row count `total`.
- **The middle-position formula handles both parities.** The two middle ranks are `FLOOR((total+1)/2)` and `FLOOR((total+2)/2)`:
  - **Odd** (`total = 7`, here): both evaluate to `4` → the single middle row, `70000`.
  - **Even** (`total = 6`): they give `3` and `4` → the two middle rows, which `AVG` then averages.
- **`AVG` finishes the job:** for an odd count it averages one row (a no-op); for an even count it averages the two middles. One formula, no `CASE` on parity.
- 💡 On MySQL 8 there is **no** `PERCENTILE_CONT` / `MEDIAN` (unlike Postgres/Oracle), so this `ROW_NUMBER` + `COUNT` pattern is the standard, portable way to compute a median.

interview-questions-interview-set-4-q3.solutionSql:
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM (
  SELECT dept, salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary) AS ranking,
    COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY dept)                 AS total
  FROM emp2
) t
WHERE ranking IN (FLOOR((total + 1) / 2),
                  FLOOR((total + 2) / 2))
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q3.explanation:
- **`PARTITION BY dept` is the only change from Q2.** It restarts the numbering *and* the count inside each department, so `ranking` and `total` are now per-department. The identical middle-position filter then finds each department's median independently.
- **Even vs odd, per group:** Eng has 4 salaries (even) → the filter keeps ranks 2 and 3 (`70000, 80000`), averaged to **75000**. Sales has 3 (odd) → it keeps rank 2 only (`60000`).
- **The outer `GROUP BY dept`** is what averages the (one or two) middle rows *per department* into a single median value each.
- 💡 This "add a `PARTITION BY`" step is the general recipe for turning any whole-table window calculation into a per-group one — median, running totals, ranks, and more.

interview-questions-interview-set-4-q4.title: Collapse consecutive check-ins into streaks
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q4.description: A gym logs each member's visit dates. Collapse each run of **consecutive** calendar days into a single streak row: `streak_start`, `streak_end`, and `streak_length`. A one-day visit is a streak of length 1.
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q4.solutionSql:
WITH ranking AS (
  SELECT member_id, visit_date,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS rn
  FROM member_checkins
),
grouped AS (
  SELECT member_id, visit_date,
    DATE_SUB(visit_date, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp
  FROM ranking
)
SELECT member_id,
  MIN(visit_date) AS streak_start,
  MAX(visit_date) AS streak_end,
  COUNT(*)        AS streak_length
FROM grouped
GROUP BY member_id, grp
ORDER BY member_id, streak_start;
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q4.explanation:
This is the **gaps-and-islands** pattern — the most-tested advanced SQL idea (streaks, consecutive logins, uptime windows all reduce to it). Both solutions assign a stable **group id** to each consecutive run, then `GROUP BY` it; they differ only in *how* they compute that id.

**Solution 1 — `date − ROW_NUMBER()`:** for a run of consecutive dates, `date − row_number` is **constant**. Number each member's visits `1, 2, 3, …` by date; consecutive dates advance in lockstep with the row number, so subtracting it lands every date in the run on the same anchor `grp`. A skipped day makes the date jump ahead of the row number, so `grp` shifts — a new island begins:

| visit_date | rn | grp (`date − rn` days) |
|------------|----|------------------------|
| 03-01 | 1 | 02-29 |
| 03-02 | 2 | 02-29 |
| 03-03 | 3 | 02-29 |
| 03-06 | 4 | 03-02 |
| 03-07 | 5 | 03-02 |
| 03-10 | 6 | 03-04 |

**Solution 2 — `LAG()` + running sum:** compare each date to the previous one with `LAG`. If the gap is exactly 1 day it's a continuation (`is_new_streak = 0`); otherwise it's a break (`= 1`). The very first row per member has `LAG = NULL` → `DATEDIFF` is `NULL` → not equal to 1 → flagged `1` (correctly starts streak #1). A **running `SUM` of those flags** then produces an increasing group id: `1,1,1,2,2,3` for M1.

- **Both then do the same finish:** each distinct `grp` is one streak — `MIN`/`MAX` give its span, `COUNT(*)` its length.
- **When to prefer which:** Solution 1 is shorter and cheaper but assumes a fixed step (consecutive *days*). Solution 2 (`LAG`) is more flexible — change the `DATEDIFF(...) = 1` condition to define "consecutive" however you like (e.g. within 7 days, or same-week), which the arithmetic trick can't express.
- 💡 The `grp` value is an internal artifact — group on it, but never expose it. For integer sequences (invoice numbers, IDs) use `value − ROW_NUMBER()` directly instead of `DATE_SUB`.

interview-questions-interview-set-4-q5.title: Matches played & winning % per team
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q5.description: Each row of `cricket_matches` records `team1`, `team2`, and the `winner`. For **every** team, report matches played, matches won, and winning percentage — remembering that a team can appear in *either* column.
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q5.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE cricket_matches (team1 VARCHAR(30), team2 VARCHAR(30), winner VARCHAR(30));

INSERT INTO cricket_matches VALUES
('India','Australia','India'),
('New Zealand','India','New Zealand'),
('India','England','India'),
('South Africa','India','India'),
('Australia','England','England'),
('India','Pakistan','Pakistan'),
('New Zealand','Australia','Australia'),
('England','India','India'),
('Pakistan','South Africa','South Africa'),
('India','New Zealand','India');
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q5.solutionSql:
WITH all_matches AS (
  SELECT team1 AS team, winner FROM cricket_matches
  UNION ALL
  SELECT team2 AS team, winner FROM cricket_matches
)
SELECT team,
  COUNT(*) AS matches_played,
  SUM(CASE WHEN team = winner THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS matches_won,
  ROUND(
    SUM(CASE WHEN team = winner THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100 / COUNT(*),
    2
  ) AS winning_percentage
FROM all_matches
GROUP BY team
ORDER BY matches_played DESC, team;
interview-questions-interview-set-4-q5.explanation:
- **The core idea: normalize two team columns into one.** A team's match can sit in either `team1` or `team2`, so a single `GROUP BY team1` would miss half its games. `UNION ALL` stacks both columns into one `team` column — now each match contributes **two** rows (one per participant), which is exactly what "matches played per team" needs. `India` surfaces in 7 matches total across both columns → `matches_played = 7`.
- **Use `UNION ALL`, not `UNION`.** `UNION` would de-duplicate identical `(team, winner)` rows and undercount teams that had the same outcome twice. You want every appearance counted, so `UNION ALL`.
- **Conditional aggregation for wins:** `SUM(CASE WHEN team = winner THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts only the rows where this team was the winner — a one-pass way to count a subset alongside the total.
- **Winning %:** `wins * 100 / played`, wrapped in `ROUND(..., 2)`. Multiplying by 100 *before* dividing keeps integer division from collapsing to 0; India = 5 × 100 / 7 = **71.43**.
- 💡 `ORDER BY matches_played DESC, team` gives the ranking-style output (busiest teams first, alphabetical within ties). In production, guard against teams with zero games via `NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0)` to avoid division-by-zero.

interview-questions-interview-set-5-q1.title: Extract name & email components
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q1.description: From free-text `full_name` and `email`, derive first name, last name, initials, the email username (before `@`), the domain (after `@`), and the top-level domain (after the last `.`).
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q1.solutionSql:
SELECT
  SUBSTRING_INDEX(full_name, ' ',  1)                   AS first_name,
  SUBSTRING_INDEX(full_name, ' ', -1)                   AS last_name,
  CONCAT(LEFT(SUBSTRING_INDEX(full_name, ' ',  1), 1),
         LEFT(SUBSTRING_INDEX(full_name, ' ', -1), 1))  AS initials,
  SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@',  1)                        AS email_user,
  SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1)                        AS email_domain,
  SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '.', -1)                        AS tld
FROM users6
ORDER BY id;
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q1.explanation:
- **`SUBSTRING_INDEX(str, delim, n)` is the whole toolkit here.** A **positive** `n` returns everything *before* the n-th delimiter (from the left); a **negative** `n` returns everything *after* the n-th-from-last delimiter. Point it at different delimiters and it does every split in this problem.
- **First vs last name:** `(full_name, ' ', 1)` grabs the first token; `(full_name, ' ', -1)` grabs the last. That's why `'Vikram Singh Rao'` → first `Vikram`, last `Rao` — the middle token is skipped by both.
- **Initials:** take `LEFT(..., 1)` of each parsed name and `CONCAT` them → `RK`, `AS`, `VR`.
- **Email split:** `(email, '@', 1)` = username, `(email, '@', -1)` = domain. **Negative counting is what makes `co.in` safe:** `(email, '.', -1)` returns only the part after the *last* dot (`in`), regardless of how many dots the domain has — a naive "split on the first dot" would break on `yahoo.co.in`.
- 💡 Caveat worth stating aloud: the first-token/last-token split is lossy for `First Middle Last` and compound surnames. To pull the **middle** token, nest the calls: `SUBSTRING_INDEX(SUBSTRING_INDEX(full_name,' ',2),' ',-1)`.

interview-questions-interview-set-5-q2.title: Longest win streak per player
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q2.description: For each player, find the length of their longest run of consecutive wins (matches ordered by match number).
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q2.solutionSql:
WITH wins AS (
  SELECT player, match_no,
    match_no - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY match_no) AS grp
  FROM matches
  WHERE result = 'W'
),
streaks AS (
  SELECT player, grp, COUNT(*) AS len
  FROM wins
  GROUP BY player, grp
)
SELECT player, MAX(len) AS longest_win_streak
FROM streaks
GROUP BY player
ORDER BY player;
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q2.explanation:
- **This is gaps-and-islands on the wins only.** First `WHERE result = 'W'` throws away losses, so only winning matches remain — but with holes in `match_no` where losses used to be.
- **`match_no − ROW_NUMBER()` labels each winning run.** Within a consecutive block of wins, both `match_no` and the row number increase by 1 in lockstep, so their difference (`grp`) stays constant. A loss creates a hole in `match_no` but not in the row number, so after the gap `grp` jumps to a new value — starting a new streak. For Kohli's wins at matches `1,2` then `4,5,6` then `8`:

  | match_no | row_number | grp |
  |----------|-----------|-----|
  | 1 | 1 | 0 |
  | 2 | 2 | 0 |
  | 4 | 3 | 1 |
  | 5 | 4 | 1 |
  | 6 | 5 | 1 |
  | 8 | 6 | 2 |

- **Two aggregations:** `COUNT(*)` per `grp` gives each streak's length (`2, 3, 1`), then `MAX(len)` per player picks the longest → Kohli **3**.
- 💡 Because we filter on wins first and use the *integer* `match_no` (not dates), this is the pure-integer form of the pattern — no `DATE_SUB` needed. Same idea powers "longest login streak", "max consecutive on-time deliveries", etc.

interview-questions-interview-set-5-q3.title: Monthly sales pivot
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q3.description: Pivot the long sales table so each product is one row with a column per month (`jan`, `feb`, `mar`); months with no sales show `0`.
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q3.solutionSql:
SELECT product,
  SUM(CASE WHEN sale_month = 'Jan' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS jan,
  SUM(CASE WHEN sale_month = 'Feb' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS feb,
  SUM(CASE WHEN sale_month = 'Mar' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS mar
FROM monthly_sales
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY product;
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q3.explanation:
- **Pivot = "rows into columns" via conditional aggregation.** MySQL has no `PIVOT` keyword, so the idiom is one aggregate per target column: `SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'X' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)`.
- **How each cell fills:** for product A, the `jan` column sums `amount` only on rows where `sale_month = 'Jan'` (100) and contributes `0` everywhere else; the `feb` column does the same for February (200); March has no A row, so its `CASE` is always `0`.
- **`GROUP BY product`** collapses each product's several month-rows into the single pivoted row. `ELSE 0` (rather than leaving `NULL`) gives clean zeros for absent months.
- 💡 This works when the columns are **known in advance**. For an unknown/large set of months you'd generate the `CASE` list dynamically (build the SQL string with `GROUP_CONCAT` + a prepared statement) — but in interviews the fixed-column version is what's expected.

interview-questions-interview-set-5-q4.title: Student marks unpivot
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q4.description: The reverse of a pivot — turn a wide marks table (one column per subject) into tall `(student, subject, marks)` rows.
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q4.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE student_marks (student VARCHAR(10), math INT, science INT, english INT);

INSERT INTO student_marks VALUES ('Amit',90,85,80),('Bob',70,60,95);
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q4.solutionSql:
SELECT student, 'Math'    AS subject, math    AS marks FROM student_marks
UNION ALL
SELECT student, 'Science',           science         FROM student_marks
UNION ALL
SELECT student, 'English',           english         FROM student_marks
ORDER BY student, FIELD(subject, 'Math', 'Science', 'English');
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q4.explanation:
- **Unpivot = "columns into rows."** MySQL has no `UNPIVOT`, so the idiom is one `SELECT` per source column, each emitting a literal subject label plus that column's value, stitched together with `UNION ALL`.
- **Why `UNION ALL`, not `UNION`:** `UNION` would deduplicate identical `(student, subject, marks)` rows — if two students genuinely scored the same, one would vanish. `UNION ALL` keeps every row, which is what you want.
- **Column names come from the first branch.** The output columns (`student, subject, marks`) are taken from the first `SELECT`; later branches just need matching positions and types, so their literals/columns don't need aliases.
- 💡 **`ORDER BY student, FIELD(subject, 'Math','Science','English')`** restores the original column order. Plain `ORDER BY subject` would sort alphabetically (English, Math, Science); `FIELD()` returns each value's position in the list, giving a custom sort that matches the source layout.

interview-questions-interview-set-5-q5.title: First & last order per customer
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q5.description: For each customer, find the date of their first and last order.
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q5.solutionSql:
SELECT customer,
  MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date,
  MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM orders5
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY customer;
interview-questions-interview-set-5-q5.explanation:
- **`MIN`/`MAX` over a date column give the earliest and latest** order per customer in a single grouped pass — no self-join or window needed. C1's three orders collapse to `2024-01-05` … `2024-03-01`; C2's single order is both its first and last.
- **`GROUP BY customer`** defines the grain — one output row per customer.
- 💡 If you need the whole first/last **order row** (order id, amount, …) rather than just the dates, `MIN`/`MAX` alone won't do it — you'd rank with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date)` for the first and `... ORDER BY order_date DESC` for the last, then keep `rn = 1`. Use the aggregate form when you only need the boundary *values*, the window form when you need the boundary *rows*.

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q1.title: Customers who ordered on consecutive days
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q1.description: Find every customer who placed orders on two or more **consecutive calendar days**.
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q1.solutionSql:
SELECT DISTINCT customer
FROM (
  SELECT customer, order_date,
    LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date) AS previous_order_date
  FROM orders6
) t
WHERE DATEDIFF(order_date, previous_order_date) = 1
ORDER BY customer;
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q1.explanation:
- **`LAG()` pulls the previous row's value onto the current row.** `PARTITION BY customer` restarts the lookback for each customer (so C2's first order never compares against C1's last), and `ORDER BY order_date` defines what "previous" means. Every row now carries both its own date and the date before it.
- **`DATEDIFF(order_date, previous_order_date) = 1` is the consecutive test.** `DATEDIFF` returns whole days between two dates, so a difference of exactly `1` means back-to-back days. C1 gets `1` twice (Jan 1→2, Jan 2→3) and `3` once (Jan 3→6); C2 gets `2` and `3` — never adjacent; C4 has a single order, so its `LAG` is `NULL`.
- **Why the subquery is required:** window functions are evaluated *after* `WHERE`, so you cannot filter on `LAG(...)` in the same `SELECT` that computes it. Wrap it in a derived table (or CTE) and filter on the outer level.
- **`DISTINCT` collapses multiple hits.** C1 satisfies the condition on two rows but should appear once. `NULL` rows (each customer's earliest order) fail the comparison automatically — `DATEDIFF(x, NULL)` is `NULL`, and `NULL = 1` is never true, so no extra `IS NOT NULL` guard is needed.
- 💡 To find customers with a streak of **3+** days rather than any 2, switch to gaps-and-islands: `DATE_SUB(order_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date) DAY)` stays constant within a run, so `GROUP BY` that expression and add `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3`.

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q2.title: Customers who purchased all products
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q2.description: Find the customers who have purchased **every** product in the catalogue.
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q2.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE purchases (
    customer VARCHAR(5),
    product VARCHAR(10)
);

INSERT INTO purchases VALUES
('C1','Laptop'),
('C1','Mouse'),
('C1','Keyboard'),

('C2','Laptop'),
('C2','Mouse'),

('C3','Laptop'),
('C3','Mouse'),
('C3','Keyboard'),

('C4','Keyboard');

CREATE TABLE products (
    product VARCHAR(10)
);

INSERT INTO products VALUES
('Laptop'),
('Mouse'),
('Keyboard');
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q2.solutionSql:
SELECT customer, COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS product_count
FROM purchases
GROUP BY customer
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product) = (
  SELECT COUNT(*)
  FROM products
)
ORDER BY customer;
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q2.explanation:
- **This is *relational division*** — "find the rows that pair with *all* values in another set." The count-matching trick is the standard SQL answer: if a customer's distinct product count equals the catalogue size, they must have bought everything.
- **`COUNT(DISTINCT product)`, not `COUNT(*)`.** If the same customer buys a Laptop twice, `COUNT(*)` would be 4 for three products and the comparison would silently fail. `DISTINCT` counts *which* products, not how many purchase rows.
- **The scalar subquery `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products)` is the target number** — here `3`. It's evaluated once, and because it's driven by the `products` table the query keeps working when the catalogue grows; nothing is hard-coded.
- **`HAVING`, not `WHERE`:** the filter compares an aggregate, and `WHERE` runs before grouping. C1 and C3 reach 3; C2 reaches 2; C4 reaches 1.
- 💡 The alternative is a **double `NOT EXISTS`** ("no product exists that this customer hasn't bought"), which is textbook-correct even when `purchases` may reference products *not* in the catalogue — a case the count method can be fooled by:

  ```sql
  SELECT DISTINCT p.customer
  FROM purchases p
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM products pr
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM purchases p2
      WHERE p2.customer = p.customer AND p2.product = pr.product
    )
  );
  ```

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q3.title: Find missing order IDs
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q3.description: `order_id` should be a gapless sequence. Report the IDs missing between the smallest and largest existing IDs.
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q3.solutionSql:
WITH RECURSIVE numbers AS (
  SELECT MIN(order_id) AS order_id
  FROM orders7

  UNION ALL

  SELECT order_id + 1
  FROM numbers
  WHERE order_id < (SELECT MAX(order_id) FROM orders7)
)
SELECT n.order_id AS missing_order_id
FROM numbers n
LEFT JOIN orders7 o
  ON n.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY n.order_id;
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q3.explanation:
- **You can't find what isn't there — so first *generate* what should be there.** The recursive CTE builds the complete sequence `101 … 107`, then an anti-join subtracts the IDs that actually exist. Missing rows are whatever's left.
- **How the recursive CTE runs:** the **anchor** `SELECT MIN(order_id)` seeds it with `101`. The **recursive member** takes the previous row and emits `order_id + 1`, repeatedly, and the `WHERE order_id < (SELECT MAX(order_id))` **stops it at 107** — without that guard it would run until MySQL's `cte_max_recursion_depth` (default 1000) aborts the query.
- **`UNION ALL`, not `UNION`:** the recursive member must not deduplicate, and `UNION` would also add pointless sort/dedup work on every iteration.
- **`LEFT JOIN … WHERE o.order_id IS NULL` is the anti-join.** Every generated number is kept; those with a match in `orders7` get a real value in `o.order_id`, those without get `NULL` — so the `IS NULL` filter keeps exactly the missing IDs, `103` and `106`.
- 💡 Note the boundary semantics: this finds gaps **inside** the observed range only. It cannot know that `100` or `108` are missing, because `MIN`/`MAX` come from the data itself. If the sequence should start at a fixed value, seed the anchor with that literal (`SELECT 100`) instead of `MIN(order_id)`. `NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders7)` is an equally valid substitute for the anti-join — but beware `NOT IN` with a `NULL`-able column, which returns no rows at all.

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q4.title: Bought product A but never B
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q4.description: Find customers who bought product **A** but have never bought product **B**.
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q4.datasetSql:
CREATE TABLE customer_products (
    customer VARCHAR(5),
    product CHAR(1)
);

INSERT INTO customer_products VALUES
('C1','A'),
('C1','B'),

('C2','A'),

('C3','B'),

('C4','A'),
('C4','C'),

('C5','A'),
('C5','B'),
('C5','C');
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q4.solutionSql:
SELECT customer
FROM customer_products
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(product = 'A') > 0
   AND SUM(product = 'B') = 0
ORDER BY customer;
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q4.explanation:
- **Both queries answer one condition per customer: "A present, B absent."** The trap is doing it row-by-row — `WHERE product = 'A' AND product <> 'B'` is always just "product = A", because a single row can't be two products at once. The test has to span *all* of a customer's rows.
- **Conditional aggregation:** in MySQL a boolean expression evaluates to `1`/`0`, so `SUM(product = 'A')` counts A-rows and `SUM(product = 'B')` counts B-rows. `> 0` means "at least one A", `= 0` means "not a single B". C1 and C5 fail the second test; C3 fails the first; C2 and C4 pass both. (`SUM(CASE WHEN product = 'A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` is the portable spelling of the same idea.)
- **`NOT EXISTS` version:** the outer query keeps only A-rows, and the correlated subquery — linked by `c2.customer = c1.customer` — asks "does this same customer have a B row?" `NOT EXISTS` keeps them only when the answer is no. It short-circuits on the first match, so it's typically the faster plan when `(customer, product)` is indexed.
- **Which to reach for:** conditional aggregation scales cleanly to compound rules (`AND SUM(product = 'C') > 0`, counts, thresholds) in one pass; `NOT EXISTS` is the more direct read of "never bought" and is the idiom to know for anti-join questions generally.
- 💡 `NOT IN (SELECT customer FROM customer_products WHERE product = 'B')` reads well too — but if that subquery can ever produce a `NULL` customer, `NOT IN` returns **zero rows**. `NOT EXISTS` is `NULL`-safe; prefer it.

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q5.title: Why can't we use `SELECT *` with `GROUP BY`?
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q5.description: Why does `SELECT * FROM employees GROUP BY dept` fail, and what's the correct way to write it?
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q5.solutionSql:
-- ❌ Fails under ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY (the MySQL 5.7+ default)
SELECT * FROM employees GROUP BY dept;

-- ✅ Every selected column is either grouped or aggregated
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS total_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q5.explanation:
- **`GROUP BY` collapses many rows into one per group — so every selected column must be answerable *for the group as a whole*.** That means each column has to be either in the `GROUP BY` list or wrapped in an aggregate (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `MIN`, …). `SELECT *` drags in `employee` and `salary`, which are neither.
- **The real problem is ambiguity, not syntax.** The `HR` group contains `Amit` and `Rohit`. Asked for one `employee` value, the engine has no defensible answer — so `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` (enabled by default since MySQL 5.7) rejects the query instead of silently inventing one.
- **Older MySQL used to allow it**, returning an arbitrary row's value per group. That's why legacy queries "work" on old servers and break after an upgrade — the data was never wrong-proof, the server just stopped guessing. Disabling `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` to make such a query run is hiding a bug, not fixing one.
- **Fix by deciding what you actually mean:** aggregate it (`MAX(salary)`), group by it (`GROUP BY dept, employee`), or — if you genuinely want *whole rows* alongside a group-level number — use a window function instead: `SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) FROM employees` keeps all four rows and attaches the per-dept count.
- 💡 `ANY_VALUE(employee)` is the escape hatch: it tells MySQL "I know this is arbitrary and I accept it," passing the check without turning the SQL mode off globally. Use it only when the column is functionally dependent on the grouping key (e.g. grouping by `employee_id` and selecting `employee_name`).

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q6.title: `DELETE` vs `TRUNCATE` vs `DROP`

rows: Removes selected rows and can use a `WHERE` clause.
Removes all rows quickly and resets the auto-increment value.
Deletes the entire table including its structure and data.

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q6.explanation:
- **The one-line framing interviewers want:** `DELETE` removes **rows you choose**, `TRUNCATE` removes **all rows**, `DROP` removes **the table**.
- **`DELETE` is DML.** It deletes row by row, writes each removal to the transaction log, fires `DELETE` triggers, and is **rollback-able** inside a transaction. That makes it the slowest option on large tables — and the only one that accepts a `WHERE`.
- **`TRUNCATE` is DDL.** MySQL implements it by dropping and recreating the table, so it's dramatically faster on big tables, but: no `WHERE`, no row-level triggers, **auto-commits** (an open transaction can't roll it back), and it **resets `AUTO_INCREMENT` to 1**. `DELETE FROM t` with no `WHERE` empties the table too but keeps the counter climbing — the classic follow-up question.
- **`DROP` is DDL and total.** Structure, data, indexes, triggers, and privileges all go; the table name no longer exists, so subsequent queries error out rather than returning zero rows. You must `CREATE TABLE` again to reuse it.
- **Foreign keys behave differently:** `TRUNCATE` is **blocked** on a table referenced by a foreign key, and `DROP` is too (unless the constraint is removed or `foreign_key_checks` is off). `DELETE` respects the constraint's `ON DELETE` action (`CASCADE`, `RESTRICT`, `SET NULL`) instead.
- 💡 Rule of thumb: **filtered delete → `DELETE`. Emptying a staging/temp table → `TRUNCATE`. Removing the object entirely → `DROP`.** Only `DELETE` is safely reversible — run the equivalent `SELECT` first, and wrap it in a transaction before touching production.

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q7.title: `IFNULL` vs `COALESCE`
interview-questions-interview-set-6-q7.description: Explain the difference between `IFNULL()` and `COALESCE()`, and use each to supply a default bonus.

rows: Returns an alternative value if the first expression is `NULL`.
Returns the first non-`NULL` value from multiple expressions.

interview-questions-interview-set-6-q7.explanation:
- **Same job, different arity.** `IFNULL(a, b)` takes **exactly two** arguments: return `a` unless it's `NULL`, else `b`. `COALESCE(a, b, c, …)` takes **any number** and returns the first non-`NULL` one, left to right. `IFNULL(a, b)` is exactly `COALESCE(a, b)`.
- **Read the rows:** for Amit, `IFNULL` jumps straight to the literal `10000` because it never sees `incentive`, while `COALESCE` finds `incentive = 1000` first and stops there. Bob has a real bonus, so both return `500`. Rahul has neither, so both fall through to `10000` — the last argument is the safety net that guarantees a non-`NULL` result.
- **`COALESCE` is standard SQL; `IFNULL` is MySQL-specific** (SQL Server's equivalent is `ISNULL`, Oracle's is `NVL`). If portability matters at all, default to `COALESCE` — it's also strictly more capable, which is why it's the better habit.
- **Short-circuit behaviour matters with expensive arguments:** both stop evaluating once they find a non-`NULL`, so put the cheap, most-likely-populated column first — especially when a later argument is a subquery.
- 💡 Two gotchas worth saying out loud. **`NULL` is not `0` or `''`** — `IFNULL(bonus, 0)` only replaces true `NULL`s, so a bonus stored as `0` stays `0`. And the **result type is the widest of the arguments**, so `COALESCE(int_col, 'N/A')` quietly returns a string and can break downstream arithmetic or sorting; keep the fallback the same type as the column. Don't confuse either with `NULLIF(a, b)`, which does the reverse — it *produces* `NULL` when `a = b`.

company-questions-company-1-q1.title: Person Who Logged In Last in Each Country
company-questions-company-1-q1.description: From the `person_logins` table, find the person (or people) who logged in **most recently** in each country.
company-questions-company-1-q1.datasetSql:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS person_logins;
CREATE TABLE person_logins (
    login_id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    person_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    country     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    login_time  DATETIME NULL
);

INSERT INTO person_logins VALUES
( 1,'Aarav Shah',    'India',   '2025-06-01 09:10:00'),
( 2,'Aarav Shah',    'India',   '2025-06-03 18:45:00'),
( 3,'Diya Nair',     'India',   '2025-06-03 21:05:00'),
( 4,'Kabir Singh',   'India',   NULL),
( 5,'Emma Clarke',   'UK',      '2025-06-02 08:00:00'),
( 6,'Oliver Hughes', 'UK',      '2025-06-04 11:30:00'),
( 7,'Emma Clarke',   'UK',      '2025-06-04 11:30:00'),
( 8,'Liam Walsh',    'Ireland', '2025-06-01 07:15:00'),
( 9,'Sofia Rossi',   'Italy',   '2025-05-30 22:40:00'),
(10,'Marco Bianchi', 'Italy',   '2025-06-02 13:00:00'),
(11,'Sofia Rossi',   'Italy',   '2025-06-01 10:00:00'),
(12,'Diya Nair',     'India',   '2025-06-02 12:00:00'),
(13,'Noah Becker',   'Germany', NULL);
company-questions-company-1-q1.solutionSql:
WITH ranked_person AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY login_time DESC) AS ranking
    FROM person_logins
    WHERE login_time IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT person_name, country, login_time
FROM ranked_person
WHERE ranking = 1
ORDER BY country, person_name;
company-questions-company-1-q1.explanation:
- `PARTITION BY country` restarts the ranking for every country, and `ORDER BY login_time DESC` puts the latest login at rank 1.
- **Why `DENSE_RANK` and not `ROW_NUMBER`:** Emma Clarke and Oliver Hughes both logged in at `2025-06-04 11:30:00` in the UK. `DENSE_RANK` gives both rank 1, so both are returned. `ROW_NUMBER` would pick one of them arbitrarily and silently drop the other.
- **Why filter `login_time IS NOT NULL`:** Germany has only a `NULL` login, and India has one too. Filtering them out means a country with no real login simply doesn't appear, instead of reporting a `NULL` as the "latest" login.
- Both methods produce the same plan. The CTE version reads top-down, which is easier to explain in an interview.

company-questions-company-1-q2.title: RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER
company-questions-company-1-q2.description: Explain the difference between `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()`, and show all three on the same data.
company-questions-company-1-q2.solutionSql:
SELECT consultant,
       utilisation_pct,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY utilisation_pct DESC, consultant_id) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY utilisation_pct DESC)                AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY utilisation_pct DESC)                AS dense_rnk
FROM consultant_scores
WHERE utilisation_pct IS NOT NULL;
company-questions-company-1-q2.explanation:
- Look at the three 88s: `RANK` gives them all 4, then **jumps to 7** for Gopal (positions 5 and 6 are "used up"). `DENSE_RANK` gives them 3 and moves on to 4.
- **Give each column its own alias.** Three columns all named `ranking` are legal in a result set but impossible to tell apart or reference later.
- **`ROW_NUMBER` needs a tie-breaker.** Without `consultant_id` in its `ORDER BY`, Ananya and Bharat can swap row numbers between runs. Adding a unique column makes the numbering repeatable.
- **Which one to use:** `ROW_NUMBER` for "exactly one row per group" (de-duplication, latest record). `DENSE_RANK` for "Nth highest value" questions (Q7). `RANK` for leaderboards where a tie should push the next person down.
- Irfan's `NULL` is filtered out. Left in, MySQL sorts `NULL` last under `DESC`, which would rank him 10th instead of excluding him.

company-questions-company-1-q3.title: Products That Were Never Sold
company-questions-company-1-q3.description: Given a `products` table and an `orders` table, list the products that have **never been ordered**.
company-questions-company-1-q3.datasetSql:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS products;
CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    category     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_id INT NULL,
    qty        INT NOT NULL,
    status     VARCHAR(12) NOT NULL,
    order_date DATE NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO products VALUES
(1,'Laptop Stand',   'Accessories'),
(2,'USB-C Hub',      'Accessories'),
(3,'Noise Headset',  'Audio'),
(4,'4K Monitor',     'Displays'),
(5,'Ergo Chair',     'Furniture'),
(6,'Webcam Pro',     'Video'),
(7,'Desk Lamp',      'Furniture'),
(8,'Wireless Mouse', 'Accessories');

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
(101, 1,    2, 'DELIVERED','2025-04-02'),
(102, 2,    1, 'DELIVERED','2025-04-03'),
(103, 1,    1, 'DELIVERED','2025-04-05'),
(104, 4,    1, 'CANCELLED','2025-04-06'),
(105, NULL, 3, 'DELIVERED','2025-04-07'),
(106, 8,    5, 'DELIVERED','2025-04-09'),
(107, 2,    2, 'RETURNED', '2025-04-10'),
(108, 99,   1, 'DELIVERED','2025-04-11'),
(109, 8,    1, 'DELIVERED','2025-04-12');
company-questions-company-1-q3.solutionSql:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.product_id = p.product_id
)
ORDER BY p.product_id;
company-questions-company-1-q3.explanation:
- **Method 1:** the `LEFT JOIN` keeps every product. Products with no order get `NULL` in every `orders` column, and `WHERE o.order_id IS NULL` keeps only those. Check a column that can never be `NULL` on a real match, like the primary key `order_id`.
- **Method 2:** `NOT EXISTS` stops at the first matching order, so it never multiplies rows. What goes in the `SELECT` inside it doesn't matter; `SELECT 1` is the convention.
- ⚠️ **Don't use `NOT IN` here.** `WHERE product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM orders)` returns **0 rows** on this data, because order 105 has a `NULL` `product_id`. `x NOT IN (…, NULL)` can never be true, so every product is filtered out. That's verified output, and it's the most common follow-up Accenture interviewers ask.
- Order 108 references product 99, which doesn't exist. It doesn't affect the result because we start from `products`.
- Product 4 was ordered but cancelled. It counts as "sold" here. If the interviewer says only delivered orders count, move `AND o.status = 'DELIVERED'` into the `ON` clause (not the `WHERE`).

company-questions-company-1-q4.title: Total Age of People Older Than 30
company-questions-company-1-q4.description: Return the number of people older than 30 and the sum of their ages. Then show the same numbers **per country**, including countries with nobody over 30.
company-questions-company-1-q4.datasetSql:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS people_profile;
CREATE TABLE people_profile (
    person_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    country   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    age       INT NULL
);

INSERT INTO people_profile VALUES
( 1,'Rahul Das',    'India',     34),
( 2,'Meera Pillai', 'India',     29),
( 3,'Vivek Menon',  'India',     30),
( 4,'Sara Khan',    'India',     41),
( 5,'Tom Price',    'UK',        52),
( 6,'Lucy Hale',    'UK',        NULL),
( 7,'Jack Wood',    'UK',        31),
( 8,'Ana Lopez',    'Spain',     27),
( 9,'Pablo Ruiz',   'Spain',     30),
(10,'Nisha Rao',    'India',     38),
(11,'Chen Wei',     'Singapore', 45);
company-questions-company-1-q4.solutionSql:
SELECT country,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN age > 30 THEN 1 END)        AS people_over_30,
       SUM(CASE WHEN age > 30 THEN age ELSE 0 END) AS total_age_over_30
FROM people_profile
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country;
company-questions-company-1-q4.explanation:
- **"Older than 30" means `> 30`, not `>= 30`.** Vivek Menon and Pablo Ruiz are exactly 30 and are excluded.
- **Why the per-country query can't use `WHERE age > 30`:** Spain has nobody over 30, so a `WHERE` filter would remove all of Spain's rows and Spain would disappear from the output. Moving the condition inside `CASE` keeps every row in the group and only counts the ones that qualify.
- `COUNT(CASE WHEN age > 30 THEN 1 END)` works because `CASE` without an `ELSE` returns `NULL`, and `COUNT` ignores `NULL`s.
- `ELSE 0` in the `SUM` makes Spain show `0` instead of `NULL`. `COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN age > 30 THEN age END), 0)` gives the same result.
- Lucy Hale's `NULL` age fails `age > 30` (the comparison is unknown, not true), so she is never counted. No extra `NULL` handling is needed.

company-questions-company-1-q5.title: PIVOT and UNPIVOT
company-questions-company-1-q5.description: Turn `quarterly_revenue` into one row per region with a column per quarter plus a total (**pivot**: rows to columns). Then turn that wide result back into one row per region per quarter (**unpivot**: columns to rows).
company-questions-company-1-q5.solutionSql:
WITH pivot_revenue AS (
    SELECT region,
           SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q1' THEN revenue END) AS q1,
           SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q2' THEN revenue END) AS q2,
           SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q3' THEN revenue END) AS q3,
           SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q4' THEN revenue END) AS q4
    FROM quarterly_revenue
    GROUP BY region
),
unpivoted AS (
    SELECT region, 'Q1' AS quarter, q1 AS revenue FROM pivot_revenue
    UNION ALL
    SELECT region, 'Q2', q2 FROM pivot_revenue
    UNION ALL
    SELECT region, 'Q3', q3 FROM pivot_revenue
    UNION ALL
    SELECT region, 'Q4', q4 FROM pivot_revenue
)
SELECT region, quarter, revenue
FROM unpivoted
WHERE revenue IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY region, quarter;
company-questions-company-1-q5.explanation:
- **MySQL has no `PIVOT` / `UNPIVOT` keywords** (SQL Server and Oracle do). The portable pattern is `SUM(CASE …)` with `GROUP BY` to pivot, and one `SELECT` per column joined with `UNION ALL` to unpivot.
- **Why `SUM` and not `MAX`:** South has two Q2 rows (60 and 45). `SUM` gives 105. `MAX` would give 60 and silently lose 45.
- **The `NULL`s are meaningful:** a `CASE` with no `ELSE` returns `NULL`, so West shows `NULL` for quarters with no revenue rather than a misleading `0`.
- **Unpivot needs `WHERE revenue IS NOT NULL`.** Without it, the `UNION ALL` produces 16 rows, including fake rows like `West, Q1, NULL` that never existed in the source. Filtering them out gives back exactly the real data.
- **A CTE only lives for one statement.** That's why the unpivot query defines `pivot_revenue` again in its own `WITH` instead of reusing it from the pivot query.
- `UNION ALL`, not `UNION`: we want every row, and `UNION` would pay for a de-duplication step it doesn't need.
- Unpivot doesn't fully reverse pivot: South's two Q2 rows come back as one row of 105. Pivoting aggregates, and aggregation can't be undone.

company-questions-company-1-q6.solutionSql:
-- 1. Look at the plan first
EXPLAIN
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE product_id = 8;

-- 2. If it shows a full scan ("Table scan on orders", or type = ALL in the
--    classic table format), add an index on the filter column
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_product_id ON orders (product_id);

-- 3. Run EXPLAIN again: it now shows
--    "Index lookup on orders using idx_orders_product_id" (type = ref)
company-questions-company-1-q6.explanation:
- **Avoid functions on indexed columns in `WHERE`.** `WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2025` can't use an index on `order_date`; `WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01'` can.
- **Indexes aren't free.** Each one slows down `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE`, and takes disk space. Index what you filter and join on, not everything.
- **Don't over-claim the `EXISTS` vs `IN` point.** Modern MySQL (8.0+) often rewrites `IN (subquery)` into the same semi-join as `EXISTS`. The real difference that always holds is `NOT IN` returning nothing when the subquery has a `NULL`.
- See [Part 13: Indexes](../docs/13-indexes.md) for composite indexes, prefix indexes and reading `EXPLAIN` output in detail.

company-questions-company-1-q7.title: Second Highest Salary in Each Department
company-questions-company-1-q7.description: Find the employee(s) with the **second highest salary** in each department.
company-questions-company-1-q7.datasetSql:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dept_salaries;
CREATE TABLE dept_salaries (
    emp_id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
    emp_name   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    department VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    salary     INT NULL
);

INSERT INTO dept_salaries VALUES
( 1,'Arjun',  'Engineering',150000),
( 2,'Bela',   'Engineering',150000),
( 3,'Chirag', 'Engineering',120000),
( 4,'Dev',    'Engineering',120000),
( 5,'Esha',   'Engineering', 90000),
( 6,'Faiz',   'Finance',    110000),
( 7,'Gita',   'Finance',     95000),
( 8,'Hari',   'Finance',      NULL),
( 9,'Ira',    'HR',          70000),
(10,'Jai',    'Sales',       80000),
(11,'Kiran',  'Sales',       72000),
(12,'Lata',   'Sales',       60000);
company-questions-company-1-q7.solutionSql:
WITH ranked_dept AS (
    SELECT emp_name, department, salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS ranking
    FROM dept_salaries
    WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT emp_name, department, salary
FROM ranked_dept
WHERE ranking = 2
ORDER BY department, emp_name;
company-questions-company-1-q7.explanation:
- **"Second highest salary" means the second highest distinct value.** In Engineering, Arjun and Bela tie at 150000, so the second highest salary is 120000, earned by Chirag and Dev. `DENSE_RANK` gets this right.
- With `ROW_NUMBER`, Bela would be "second" (150000), which is wrong. With `RANK`, the 120000 earners get rank 3 and `ranking = 2` returns nothing for Engineering.
- **HR is missing on purpose.** Ira is the only person in HR, so there is no second highest salary.
- Hari's `NULL` salary is filtered out so it can't occupy a rank.
- Change `ranking = 2` to `ranking = N` for the Nth highest, or `ranking <= 3` for the top 3 per department.

company-questions-company-1-q8.title: Find and Remove Duplicate Rows By email
company-questions-company-1-q8.description: Find emails that appear more than once in `customer_signups`, then delete the duplicates while **keeping the earliest signup** (lowest `signup_id`) for each email.
company-questions-company-1-q8.datasetSql:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS customer_signups;
CREATE TABLE customer_signups (
    signup_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    email       VARCHAR(40) NULL,
    full_name   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    signup_date DATE NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO customer_signups VALUES
(1,'asha@mail.com',  'Asha',  '2025-01-05'),
(2,'ravi@mail.com',  'Ravi',  '2025-01-06'),
(3,'ASHA@mail.com ', 'Asha',  '2025-01-09'),
(4,'meena@mail.com', 'Meena', '2025-01-10'),
(5,'ravi@mail.com',  'Ravi',  '2025-01-06'),
(6,'ravi@mail.com',  'Ravi',  '2025-01-12'),
(7, NULL,            'Tarun', '2025-01-13'),
(8, NULL,            'Uma',   '2025-01-14'),
(9,'john@mail.com',  'John',  '2025-01-15');
company-questions-company-1-q8.explanation:
- **Clean the key before comparing it.** Row 3 is `'ASHA@mail.com '`, with capitals and a trailing space. Grouping on the raw `email` only finds `ravi@mail.com` (verified), because MySQL 8's default collation ignores case but **not** trailing spaces. `LOWER(TRIM(email))` catches the Asha duplicate too. Real signup data always has this kind of mess, so interviewers like to see you handle it.
- **How the `DELETE` works:** the self-join pairs each row with every row that has the same email and a **smaller** `signup_id`. Any row that finds such a partner is a later duplicate and gets deleted. The row with the lowest id has no smaller partner, so it survives.
- **`NULL` emails are left alone.** `NULL = NULL` is not true, so Tarun and Uma never pair up and neither is deleted. That's correct: two missing emails aren't evidence of a duplicate customer.
- **Always run Step 1 (or a `SELECT` version of Step 2) before the `DELETE`**, and do it inside a transaction on real data. A wrong join condition here deletes good rows with no undo.
- **Alternative with a window function:**

  ```sql
  DELETE FROM customer_signups
  WHERE signup_id IN (
      SELECT signup_id FROM (
          SELECT signup_id,
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) ORDER BY signup_id) AS rn
          FROM customer_signups
          WHERE email IS NOT NULL
      ) t
      WHERE rn > 1
  );
  ```

  The extra derived table `t` is required: MySQL won't let a `DELETE` read directly from the table it is deleting from in a subquery.

company-questions-company-1-q9.title: Row Counts for Each Join Type on val
company-questions-company-1-q9.description: Two tables are joined on `val`. Both have duplicate values and `NULL`s. How many rows does each join type return? Write one query that shows all the counts.
company-questions-company-1-q9.solutionSql:
SELECT 'INNER' AS join_type, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM join_left_vals l
JOIN join_right_vals r ON l.val = r.val

UNION ALL

SELECT 'LEFT', COUNT(*)
FROM join_left_vals l
LEFT JOIN join_right_vals r ON l.val = r.val

UNION ALL

SELECT 'RIGHT', COUNT(*)
FROM join_left_vals l
RIGHT JOIN join_right_vals r ON l.val = r.val

UNION ALL

-- MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN: LEFT JOIN rows + right rows with no match
SELECT 'FULL OUTER',
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM join_left_vals l LEFT JOIN join_right_vals r ON l.val = r.val)
     + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM join_right_vals r
        WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM join_left_vals l WHERE l.val = r.val))

UNION ALL

SELECT 'CROSS', COUNT(*)
FROM join_left_vals l
CROSS JOIN join_right_vals r;
company-questions-company-1-q9.explanation:
Work it out by hand first. That's what the interviewer is really testing.

| val | Left rows | Right rows | Matched pairs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 3 | 2 × 3 = **6** |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 × 1 = **1** |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 (left only) |
| 4 | 0 | 1 | 0 (right only) |
| NULL | 1 | 1 | 0 (`NULL = NULL` is not true) |

- **INNER = 7:** only matched pairs, 6 + 1. Duplicates multiply: each of the two left 1s joins to all three right 1s.
- **LEFT = 9:** 7 matched + 2 unmatched left rows (val 3 and the left `NULL`).
- **RIGHT = 9:** 7 matched + 2 unmatched right rows (val 4 and the right `NULL`).
- **FULL OUTER = 11:** 7 matched + 2 left-only + 2 right-only. MySQL doesn't support `FULL OUTER JOIN`, so it's built from a `LEFT JOIN` plus the right rows that have no match.
- **CROSS = 30:** every left row with every right row, 5 × 6. No join condition, so `NULL`s don't matter.
- **The `NULL` rows never match each other** in any join with `=`. They only appear as unmatched rows in outer joins.

company-questions-company-1-q10.title: Rolling 7-Day Average of Daily Orders
company-questions-company-1-q10.description: Calculate the **rolling 7-day average** of daily order amounts. Days with no orders must count as 0.
company-questions-company-1-q10.solutionSql:
WITH RECURSIVE daily_sales AS (
    SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
    FROM daily_orders
    GROUP BY order_date
),
calendar AS (
    SELECT MIN(order_date) AS order_date
    FROM daily_sales

    UNION ALL

    SELECT DATE_ADD(order_date, INTERVAL 1 DAY)
    FROM calendar
    WHERE order_date < (SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM daily_sales)
)
SELECT c.order_date,
       COALESCE(d.total_amount, 0) AS total_amount,
       ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(d.total_amount, 0)) OVER (
           ORDER BY c.order_date
           RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ), 2) AS rolling_7d_avg
FROM calendar c
LEFT JOIN daily_sales d
       ON c.order_date = d.order_date
ORDER BY c.order_date;
company-questions-company-1-q10.explanation:
- **Step 1, `daily_sales`:** collapse to one row per day. The table has several orders per day, and a window over raw rows would treat "previous 6 rows" as "previous 6 orders", not days.
- **Step 2, `calendar`:** a recursive CTE generates every date from the first to the last order date, including the gap days 03-05 and 03-09. `WITH RECURSIVE` must be written once at the start, even though only `calendar` is recursive.
- **Step 3:** `LEFT JOIN` the calendar to the daily totals, so gap days get `0` via `COALESCE`, then average over the current day plus the 6 before it.
- ⚠️ **Skip the calendar and the average is wrong.** Windowing only over days that have orders, 03-06's "7-day" average becomes **1197.00** instead of **997.50**, because the empty day 03-05 is missing and the window quietly reaches back an extra day. That's verified output.
- **`RANGE … INTERVAL 6 DAY` vs `ROWS 6 PRECEDING`:** once the calendar has no gaps, both give the same result here. `RANGE` is the safer choice because it measures in days, not rows, so it stays correct even if a date were ever missing.
- The first 6 days have partial windows (03-01 averages only itself). If a partial window is misleading for your report, filter out rows before the 7th day.
- For the full progression of rolling-window patterns, see [Bonus Set 1: The Rolling Sum Pattern](../bonus-problems/set-01-rolling-sum-pattern.md).

company-questions-company-1-q11.solutionSql:
-- WHERE filters rows
SELECT emp_id, emp_name, department
FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Sales';

-- HAVING filters groups
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS total_count
FROM employees
WHERE department IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) < 3;
company-questions-company-1-q11.explanation:
- `WHERE COUNT(*) < 3` is an error: when `WHERE` runs, the groups don't exist yet, so there is nothing to count.
- The second query uses **both**: `WHERE` first removes the rows with no department, then `HAVING` filters the groups that are left.
- **Rule of thumb:** if a condition can go in `WHERE`, put it there. Filtering rows before grouping is cheaper than grouping everything and filtering afterwards (see Q6).

company-questions-company-1-q12.solutionSql:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS total_count
FROM employees
WHERE department IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY total_count DESC;
company-questions-company-1-q12.explanation:
- `GROUP BY department` makes one group per department, `COUNT(*)` counts the rows in each, and `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5` keeps only the large ones.
- **"More than 5" is `> 5`.** Sales has exactly 5 employees and is correctly excluded.
- ⚠️ **Why `WHERE department IS NOT NULL` matters:** six employees have no department. `GROUP BY` puts all `NULL`s into one group, so without the filter a row `NULL | 6` appears in the result (verified). "Unassigned" isn't a department.
